etymology: from ultimate + -ly; ultimate from Latin ultimatus 'last', from ultimus 'farthest, last'.

similar.description: ultimate is adjective; ultimately is the adverb 'in the end'.

examples: They issued an ultimatum to withdraw.
etymology: from Latin ultimatum 'a final thing', neuter of ultimatus 'last' (ultimus 'last').

similar.description: both from Latin ultimus 'last'; ultimatum is a final demand.

etymology: from ultra- 'beyond' + sonic (from Latin sonus 'sound'); beyond audible sound.

similar.description: supersonic is faster than sound; ultrasonic is above hearing range.

etymology: from un- 'not' + called-for (summoned/needed); not invited or warranted.

similar.description: both mean not justified; uncalled-for implies not invited.

memory_tip: un(不)+called-for(被需要的)，'不必要的/无端的'。

examples: He uncapped the pen and wrote.
etymology: from un- 'reverse' + cap; cap from Latin cappa 'hood'.

similar.description: both mean to remove a cover; uncap specifically removes a cap.

etymology: from un- 'not' + conditional (from Latin condicio 'agreement, terms').

similar.description: conditional has terms; unconditional has none.

examples: He was unconscious of the danger.
etymology: from un- 'not' + conscious (Latin conscius 'knowing with', from con- + scire 'to know').

similar.description: subconscious is below awareness; unconscious is lacking awareness.

etymology: from un- 'not' + deniable (from Latin denegare 'to deny').

similar.description: deny is to refuse; undeniable means cannot be denied.

etymology: from under- 'insufficiently' + charge (from Late Latin carricare 'to load').

similar.description: overcharge is the opposite, charging too much.

etymology: from under- + write; originally to sign one's name under a document as guarantor.

similar.description: underwriter is one who underwrites, esp. an insurer.

memory_tip: under(在…下)+write(写)，'签名担保'即承保。

examples: He gave the matter undue attention.
etymology: from Middle English undue 'not owed', from un- 'not' + due (Latin debitus 'owed').

similar.description: due is owed/proper; undue is excessive or improper.

memory_tip: un(不)+due(应得的)，'过度的/不适当的'。

examples: The snake undulated across the sand.
etymology: from Latin undulatus 'wavy', from unda 'wave' + -ulus (diminutive).

similar.description: undulation is the noun 'a wave-like motion'.
undulate means to move in waves.

etymology: from undue + -ly; undue from un- 'not' + due 'proper'.

similar.description: undue is adjective; unduly is the adverb.

examples: The teams were uneven in skill.
etymology: from un- 'not' + even (Old English efen 'flat, equal').

similar.description: even is level/equal; uneven is not.

etymology: from un- 'not' + gainly (from Old Norse gegn 'straight, fitting'); not graceful.

similar.description: gainly (graceful) is rare; ungainly is its negative.

examples: The unicorn is a mythical beast.
A unicorn appeared in the tale.
etymology: from Latin unicornis 'having one horn', from uni- 'one' + cornu 'horn'.

similar.description: uni- is the Latin prefix for one, as in uniform, unilateral.

etymology: from uni- 'one' + lateral (Latin lateralis 'of the side', from latus 'side').

similar.description: bilateral is two-sided; unilateral is one-sided.

etymology: from un- 'not' + official (from Latin officium 'duty, office').

similar.description: official is authorized; unofficial is not.

etymology: from un- 'reverse' + ravel (to tangle); to disentangle.

similar.description: ravel means to tangle; unravel reverses it (un-tangle).

examples: Social unrest grew in the city.
etymology: from un- 'not' + rest (Old English ræst 'quiet'); lack of peace.

similar.description: rest is calm; unrest is its absence, turmoil.

etymology: from un- 'not' + thinkable (from think + -able).

similar.description: thinkable can be conceived; unthinkable cannot.

etymology: from un- 'not' + told (past of tell); not counted/narrated, hence immense.

similar.description: told is recounted; untold is not told, or too great to count.

memory_tip: un(未)+told(讲述/数)，'数不清的/极大的'。

etymology: from up + to + date (from Latin data 'given', in 'date given'); current to the present.

similar.description: updated is made current; up-to-date is being current.

etymology: from up- + bringing (noun of bring up); the rearing of a child.

similar.description: bring up a child = give them their upbringing.

examples: The chair was upholstered in velvet.
etymology: from upholsterer, from Middle English upholder 'a dealer who displays goods', from up- + hold.

similar.description: both from up- + hold; upholster originally 'to hold up/furnish' goods.

examples: The upkeep of the garden is costly.
They share the upkeep of the road.
etymology: from up- + keep; the act of keeping something in good condition.

similar.description: keep is maintain; upkeep is the maintaining/nursing of something.

examples: He was an urbane and witty host.
She spoke in an urbane manner.
etymology: from Latin urbanus 'of the city, refined', from urbs 'city'.

similar.description: urban relates to the city; urbane means city-refined, polished.
urbane vs suburban, both from urbs 'city'.

memory_tip: urb(城市)+ane，城市人'温文尔雅的'。

examples: The tool has little practical utility.
etymology: from Latin utilitas 'usefulness', from utilis 'useful' (uti 'to use').

similar.description: utilize is to use; utility is usefulness or a public service.
utility shares root with utilitarian (usefulness-based).

etymology: from utter (Old English ūtera 'outer, complete') + -ly; to the utmost.

similar.description: utter as verb means to speak; as adjective means total (utterly).

etymology: from Latin vacantia 'emptiness', from vacare 'to be empty' (vas 'empty').

similar.description: vacant is adjective 'empty'; vacancy is the noun.
both from vacare 'to be empty/free'; vacation is free time.

etymology: from Latin vaccinus 'of a cow' (vacca 'cow'); first developed from cowpox by Jenner.

similar.description: vaccine(疫苗)与vacuum(真空)拼写相近但源不同。

memory_tip: 源于拉丁 vacca(牛)，牛痘疫苗。

examples: The validity of the argument was questioned.
etymology: from Latin validitas 'strength', from validus 'strong' (valēre 'to be strong').

similar.description: valid is adjective; validity is the noun 'soundness'.

examples: The valuation set the price at £1m.
etymology: from Latin valere 'to be worth' + -ation; the act of estimating worth.

similar.description: value is worth; valuation is the assessment of worth.

etymology: from Old French venquis, past participle of veintre 'to conquer', from Latin vincere 'to conquer'.

similar.description: both mean to defeat; vanquish is more literary.
vanquish(征服)与vanish(消失)拼写相近易混。

examples: Water vapor rose from the lake.
etymology: from Latin vapor 'steam, heat', from Proto-Italic *wapōr.

similar.description: vapour is the British spelling; vapor the American.
vaporize is to turn into vapor.

examples: This is a variant of the flu virus.
etymology: from Latin varians 'varying', from variare 'to change' (varius 'diverse').

similar.description: variation is the act/changing; variant is a differing form.

etymology: from Latin variare 'to change' + -ed; having many forms.

similar.description: various means several different; varied means showing variety.

examples: The leaves were variegated green and white.
A variegated pattern covered the cloth.
etymology: from Latin variegatus 'diversified in color', from varius 'varied' + agere 'to make'.

similar.description: both from varius; variegated emphasizes mixed colors.

examples: The wine fermented in a vat.
The dye was mixed in a large vat.
etymology: from Old English fæt 'vat, vessel', of Germanic origin.

similar.description: vat(大桶)与bat(蝙蝠)拼写相近易混。

examples: She was vehement in her denial.
etymology: from Latin vehemens 'impetuous, violent', perhaps from ve- 'without' + root of mēns 'mind'.

similar.description: both intense; vehement is passionate intensity, often of feeling.

examples: The venerable old man advised them.
etymology: from Latin venerabilis 'worthy of reverence', from venerari 'to worship' (Venus 'goddess').

similar.description: venerate is the verb; venerable is the adjective 'revered'.

etymology: from Latin venerari 'to worship, revere', from venus 'favor, love'.

similar.description: venerable is the adjective; venerate the verb 'to revere'.

examples: He sought vengeance for the wrong.
They took vengeance on their enemy.
etymology: from Latin vindicta 'revenge', from vimdicare 'to claim, avenge'; via Old French vengeance.

similar.description: both mean retaliation; vengeance is the act/desire, revenge the act done.

memory_tip: veng(报)+eance，'复仇'如 vindicate 维权。

examples: The chimney is a vent for smoke.
She vented her anger on him.
etymology: from Latin ventus 'wind'; an opening for air; in 'vent anger' from vent (to let out).

similar.description: ventilate is to air out; vent is the opening or to release.
vent(排气口)与vent(冒险的)注意多义。

memory_tip: vent 源于'wind(风)'，'通风口/发泄'。

etymology: from Latin ventilatio 'a fanning', from ventilare 'to expose to wind' (ventus 'wind').

similar.description: vent is the opening; ventilation is the airing system.

examples: The poem was written in the vernacular.
etymology: from Latin vernaculus 'domestic, native', from verna 'home-born slave'.

similar.description: vernacular(方言)与vernal(春天的)拼写相近同根verna。

examples: She is well versed in law.
He is versed in several languages.
etymology: from Latin versari 'to be engaged in, turn', from vertere 'to turn'; skilled through practice.

similar.description: versed means skilled/knowledgeable, often 'well versed in'.

memory_tip: vers(转/从事)+ed，'精通的'(常接 in)。

examples: The veterinary clinic treated the dog.
etymology: from Latin veterinarius 'of beasts of burden', from veterinae 'cattle' (vetus 'old').

similar.description: veterinary(兽医的)与veteran(老兵)拼写相近同根vetus(老)。

examples: She was vexed by the delay.
etymology: from Latin vexare 'to shake, trouble, annoy'.

similar.description: vex(使烦恼)与anxious(焦虑的)拼写相近。

memory_tip: vex 源于拉丁'摇动/困扰'，'使苦恼'。

examples: The business became viable last year.
etymology: from French viable 'capable of living', from Latin vita 'life' + -able.

similar.description: both from Latin vita 'life'; viable = able to live, vital = of life.

examples: Sound is a vibration of air.
etymology: from Latin vibratio 'a shaking', from vibrare 'to shake, quiver'.

similar.description: vibrate is the verb; vibration the noun.

etymology: from Latin vigilans 'awake, watchful', from vigil 'awake' (vigēre 'to be lively').

similar.description: vigil is a period of wakeful observation; vigilant is watchful.

etymology: from Latin vindicare 'to claim, avenge, set free', from vim 'force' + dicare 'to declare'.

similar.description: vindicate(证明无罪)与vindictive(报复心的)同根但义不同。

examples: Ivy climbed the wall like a vine.
etymology: from Latin vīnea 'vineyard', from vīnum 'wine'; a climbing plant.

similar.description: wine and vine both from Latin vīnum; the plant that makes wine.

memory_tip: vine 即'藤/葡萄藤'，联想 wine 葡萄酒。

examples: They toured a vineyard in France.
etymology: from vine + yard; yard from Old English geard 'enclosure'.

similar.description: vine is the plant; vineyard is the planted field.

examples: The leader projected a virile image.
etymology: from Latin virilis 'of a man', from vir 'man'.

similar.description: both from Latin vir 'man'; virtue originally 'manliness'.

etymology: from Latin virtuosus, from virtus 'goodness, manliness', from vir 'man'.

similar.description: virtue is the quality; virtuous is the adjective.

etymology: from visual (Latin visualis, from videre 'to see') + -ize.

similar.description: visual is of sight; visualize is to form a mental image.

etymology: from Latin vocatio 'a calling', from vocare 'to call' (vox 'voice').

similar.description: vocation is a calling/career; vocational relates to career training.

etymology: from French vogue 'fashion', from Italian voga 'a rowing, course', from vogare 'to row'.

similar.description: vogue(时尚)与vague(模糊的)拼写相近易混。

etymology: from Latin volatilis 'flying, swift', from volare 'to fly'.

similar.description: volatility is the noun; volatile means changeable/unstable.

memory_tip: vol(飞)+atile，像飞一样'易变的/不稳定的'。

etymology: from volcano + -ic; volcano from Italian vulcano, from Latin Vulcanus 'Vulcan (god of fire)'.

similar.description: volcano is the mountain; volcanic is the adjective.

etymology: from Latin voluptuosus 'pleasing', from voluptas 'pleasure' (velle 'to wish').

similar.description: voluptuous(丰满的/感官的)与voluntary(自愿的)拼写相近但义不同。

examples: The child vomited after the meal.
etymology: from Latin vomitare 'to throw up', from vomere 'to spew'.

similar.description: vomit(呕吐)与vowel(元音)拼写相近易混。

examples: He was drawn into a vortex of debt.
etymology: from Latin vortex 'a whirl, eddy', variant of vertex 'to turn' (vertere 'to turn').

similar.description: vortex(漩涡)与vertex(顶点)同源但拼写相近。

examples: Bring the voucher to redeem it.
He gave her a gift voucher.
etymology: from Anglo-French voucher 'to call, summon', from Latin vocare 'to call'.

similar.description: vouch is to guarantee; voucher is the proof/coupon.

etymology: from Latin votum 'a vow, promise', from vovere 'to vow'.

similar.description: vow(誓言)与vowel(元音)拼写相近易混。

etymology: from Anglo-French wagier 'to pledge', of Germanic origin related to wage.

similar.description: wager and wage both from a root meaning a pledge/stake.
wager(打赌)与vague(模糊的)拼写相近。

etymology: from Middle English wailen, of imitative origin (cry of lament).

similar.description: wail(哀嚎)与whale(鲸鱼)同音易混。
wail(哭)与wale(鞭痕/凸纹)拼写相近。

examples: The wallaby hopped across the field.
A wallaby is smaller than a kangaroo.
etymology: from Dharuk (Australian Aboriginal) walabi, name of the animal.

similar.description: wallaby is a smaller relative of the kangaroo.

memory_tip: wallaby 即'小袋鼠'(澳洲土著语)。

etymology: from Old English wanian 'to decrease', of Germanic origin.

similar.description: wax (grow) and wane (shrink) describe the moon's cycles.
wane(衰退)与wine(酒)拼写相近。

memory_tip: wane 与 wax 相对，'衰退/亏缺'(月亏)。

examples: The prison warden inspected the cells.
etymology: from Old French wardein 'guardian', from warder 'to guard' (Germanic).

similar.description: ward is protection; warden is the guardian/officer.
warden shares ward- 'guard' with wardrobe.

examples: The TV comes with a one-year warranty.
etymology: from warrant + -y; warrant from Old North French warant 'protector, guarantee'.

similar.description: warrant is a guarantee/justification; warranty is the written guarantee.
both mean a promise of quality; warranty is the document.

examples: He was a warrior in the tribe.
etymology: from war + -ior (agent suffix, from Latin -or); one who wages war.

similar.description: war is conflict; warrior is the fighter.

examples: She was wary after the scam.
etymology: from ware 'cautious' (Old English wær) + -y; related to beware.

similar.description: wary(警惕的)与weary(疲倦的)拼写相近易混。
both from the same root meaning 'watchful'.

memory_tip: war(防)+y，'小心的/警惕的'(beware 同源)。

examples: The wasp buzzed around the jam.
etymology: from Old English wæps, from Proto-Germanic *wapsō; imitative of buzzing.

similar.description: wasp is slender with a narrow waist; bee is fuzzy and rounder.

memory_tip: wasp 即'黄蜂'，拟声嗡嗡声。

examples: He did not waver in his decision.
The flame wavered in the wind.
etymology: from wave + -er (frequentative); to move waveringly.

similar.description: wave is a motion; waver is to flicker/hesitate.

etymology: from Old English wēnian 'to accustom', of Germanic origin.

similar.description: wean means to detach from a habit or milk, accustom away.

etymology: from well + to + do; 'doing well' financially.

similar.description: both mean rich; well-to-do is milder, comfortable.

memory_tip: well(好)+to do(做)，'富裕的/小康的'。

examples: Return to the place whence you came.
etymology: from Old English hwanon 'from what place', from hwa 'who' + -on (from).

similar.description: hence = from here; whence = from where (archaic).
whence(从何处)与where(哪里)拼写相近。

examples: The law whereby rights are protected.
etymology: from where + by; by which means.

similar.description: wherein = in which; whereby = by which.

etymology: from Middle English whilest, from while + -st (adverbial suffix); British for 'while'.

similar.description: whilst is the British formal equivalent of while.

etymology: from whirl + wind; a rotating column of air.

similar.description: whirl is to spin; whirlwind is the spinning wind.
both rotating winds; whirlwind is smaller, local.

examples: Whiting is a type of fish.
etymology: from Middle English whiting, from white (its pale color) + -ing.

similar.description: whiting is also powdered chalk/white lead used in paint.
named for its white color.

etymology: from whole + sale; selling in complete quantities, not retail.

similar.description: retail is selling to consumers; wholesale is in bulk to sellers.

etymology: from Old English wieldan 'to control, use', of Germanic origin.

similar.description: wield(挥舞/掌握)与yield(屈服/产出)拼写相近易混。

etymology: frequentative of wig (to move), from Middle English wiglen, of imitative origin.

similar.description: wiggle is a small, rapid side-to-side movement.
wiggle(扭动)与jiggle(轻摇)拼写/义相近。

etymology: from wild + -erness (noun suffix, as in darkness); a wild uncultivated area.

similar.description: wild is adjective; wilderness is the wild land.

examples: The flowers withered in the heat.
etymology: from Middle English wideren, from Old English windan 'to twist' (withering like twisting dry).

similar.description: wither(枯萎)与weather(天气)拼写相近。

memory_tip: wither 联想'风(wind)吹干'而'枯萎'。

examples: The baby grew in the womb.
etymology: from Old English wamb 'belly, womb', of Germanic origin.

similar.description: womb(子宫)与tomb(坟墓)拼写/发音相近易混。

examples: Check the wording of the contract.
etymology: from word + -ing; the choice/arrangement of words.

similar.description: word is a unit; wording is how words are put together.

examples: He is a workaholic who never rests.
etymology: blend of work + -aholic (from alcoholic, implying addiction).

similar.description: -aholic suffix borrowed from alcoholic, implying compulsion.

examples: They wreathed the door with flowers.
etymology: from wreathe, from Old English wrīthan 'to twist', of Germanic origin.

similar.description: wreath is the ring of flowers; wreathe is to twist/encircle.

memory_tip: wreath(花环)+e，'环绕/笼罩'(扭绕成环)。

examples: The boys wrestled on the grass.
etymology: from Old English wræstlian, from wræstan 'to twist, wrench'.

similar.description: wrestle(摔跤)与wrest(夺取/拧)同根，拼写相近。
wrestling is the sport of wrestle.

etymology: past participle of work (Old English worht); originally 'worked', now mostly in wrought iron.

similar.description: wrought is the archaic past of work; used in 'wrought iron'.

memory_tip: wrought 是 work 的古过去分词，'锻的'。

etymology: coined by Roentgen (1895); X for the unknown radiation + ray.

similar.description: ray is a beam; X-ray uses unknown 'X' radiation.

examples: They sailed the yacht to the island.
etymology: from Dutch jacht 'a fast light ship', short for jachtschip 'pursuit ship' (jagen 'to hunt').

similar.description: yacht is pronounced 'yot'; the -cht is silent, often misspelled.

memory_tip: yacht 源自荷兰语'猎船'，'游艇'(ch不发音)。

etymology: from Old English giernan 'to desire', of Germanic origin.

similar.description: yearn(渴望)与yarn(纱线/故事)拼写相近易混。
yearn 与 burn 仅首字母差，注意拼写。

etymology: from Old English gelp 'boasting', later a sharp cry; imitative.

similar.description: yell is a loud cry; yelp is a short sharp one (often pain).

memory_tip: yelp 拟声'短促尖叫'如狗叫。

examples: The oxen were put under the yoke.
They threw off the yoke of tyranny.
etymology: from Old English geoc 'yoke', from Proto-Indo-European *yugom 'to join' (as in join/yoke).

similar.description: yoke(轭)与yolk(蛋黄)同音易混。
yoga and yoke both from the root meaning 'to join'.

memory_tip: yoke 即'轭'，与 join 同根(连接)。

examples: She added zest to the dish.
etymology: from French zeste 'orange peel', used for flavor; later 'keen enjoyment'.

similar.description: zest(热情/风味)与zeal(热心)拼写/义相近。
zest 与 pest 仅首字母差。

memory_tip: zest 源自'橙皮'(提味)，引申'热情/风味'。
